name: Forestry & Timber Management

objectives.text: Identify products that come from trees, such as lumber, paper, and fruit
Identify the main parts of a tree, including roots, trunk, bark, branches, and leaves, and describe what each part does for the tree
Sort trees into deciduous and coniferous groups using their leaves, needles, and seeds
Describe the difference between a forest that is planted and managed and one that grows wild
Explain why timber is a renewable resource by tracing a managed forest from seedling through harvest and replanting
Demonstrate the correct way to plant a tree seedling, including hole depth, root placement, and spacing
Identify common local trees using leaf shape, leaf arrangement, and leaf margin
Measure the diameter at breast height of a tree and estimate its age by counting growth rings
Explain how wildfire, insects, disease, and overcrowding affect the health of a forest
Describe the work of forestry careers such as forester, logger, sawmill operator, and urban forester
Explain how practices such as thinning, selective harvest, and clear-cutting each affect a forest's health and regrowth
Identify tree and woody plant species by leaf, bark, twig, bud, and fruit characteristics as used in the FFA Forestry CDE
Identify the characteristics of a healthy forest stand, including species diversity, crown vigor, stocking level, and absence of pest damage
Use a Biltmore stick and Merritt hypsometer to measure tree diameter and merchantable height in logs
Demonstrate safe operation and maintenance practices for chainsaws and other forestry tools
Explain how harvested logs are processed into forest products such as lumber, plywood, pulp, and biomass fuel
Conduct a timber cruise using fixed plots or a prism to estimate the board foot volume and growth rate of a stand
Compare forest harvesting systems such as clear-cut, seed tree, shelterwood, and single-tree selection for regeneration, cost, and site suitability
Compare sustainable forestry practices such as timber stand improvement, release cutting, pruning, prescribed fire, and reforestation for their effect on stand quality
Identify common tree defects and apply a log rule to scale and grade sawlogs
Calculate the stumpage value of a timber stand using volume estimates and current market prices
Analyze a forest stand to determine which forestry techniques would improve its habitat and timber quality
Create a timber stand improvement plan for a woodlot that prescribes specific treatments and their timing
Devise a forest management plan that improves habitat while optimizing the quantity or quality of harvestable timber
Develop a timber harvest plan that balances economic yield, wildlife habitat, and long-term forest sustainability

changes: Kept and lightly reworded all six existing objectives. Converted the grade 12 evaluation of a harvest plan into developing one, to match NRS.03.01.01.c. Added early competencies: tree parts, deciduous vs coniferous, the renewable forest cycle, seedling planting, leaf-based identification, forest health threats, and forestry careers. Added high school competencies tied to the Forestry CDE and SAE: species identification, healthy stand traits, Biltmore stick and hypsometer use, chainsaw safety, forest products processing, timber cruising, harvest system comparison, TSI and sustainable practice comparison, log scaling and grading, stumpage valuation, stand analysis, and TSI and management plans. Excluded the wildlife and aquatic harvest standards because they belong to sibling sub-topics.
